chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ahmad ibn al-Walid (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated to us, saying: Sa'd ibn Abdullah narrated to us, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad al-Isbahani, from al-Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Manqari, from Ali ibn Hashim al-Bareed, from his father, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), that a man asked him about abstinence.

He said: Abstinence is ten things. The highest ranks of abstinence are the lowest ranks of piety, and the highest ranks of piety are the lowest ranks of certainty, and the highest ranks of certainty are the lowest ranks of satisfaction.
Indeed, abstinence is in a verse from the Book of Allah, Exalted and Glorious is He: 'So that you will not despair over what has eluded you nor rejoice over what He has given you.'

key_terms.الرِّضَا: Satisfaction or contentment with divine decree.
key_terms.الزُّهْد: Abstinence or asceticism, defined here as a spiritual state of detachment and balance.
key_terms.الْوَرَع: Piety or God-consciousness, specifically caution against sin and doubt.
key_terms.الْيَقِين: Certainty or conviction, a high spiritual station of knowing God.
key_terms.لِكَيْلَا تَأْسَوْا: So that you will not despair, a key phrase from Surah Al-Hadid.

ai.seo_question: What is the spiritual definition of abstinence (zuhd) in Shia hadith and how is it linked to Quranic verses?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Saduq records Imam al-Baqir’s definition of zuhd as a progressive spiritual ladder culminating in rida (contentment), explicitly linking it to the concept of wara' (piety) and yaqin (certainty). By grounding this hierarchy in Surah Al-Hadid 57:23, the Imam emphasizes that true asceticism is not merely material poverty but an internal state of emotional equilibrium—neither despairing over loss nor exulting in gain—which reflects deep theological certainty. This interpretation aligns with the Shia emphasis on inner purification (tazkiyah) as the essence of worship, moving beyond superficial renunciation to a sustained state of divine satisfaction.
